questions.stem: A content marketer asks Claude, with web search on, for statistics to support a blog post about remote work. Claude returns the line "68% of employees say flexible hours make them more productive" and cites a news article. When she opens the article, it attributes the figure to a survey by a research institute but does not link to it. The post goes live on the company website next week. What is the MOST reliable way to validate the statistic before publishing?

options.text: Keep the news article as the citation, since a published outlet reporting the figure is a reasonable source for a blog.
Find the institute's original survey report and confirm the figure, the question asked, the sample and the year.
Ask Claude to search again and confirm the figure appears on at least three other websites before using it.
Soften the sentence to "most employees" so that the post no longer depends on the exact percentage.

questions.explanation: A news article that reports a survey figure is a **secondary** source. Only the research institute's original report can confirm that the number is right and that it means what the blog will say it means — who was asked, what exactly they were asked, and when. Validating a factual claim bound for publication means checking it against the authoritative source, not against whoever repeated it.

whyWrong.A: The outlet only repeats the figure. If it misquoted the survey or cut out its context, the blog would repeat the error under the company's name.
whyWrong.C: Statistics are often copied from site to site. Three pages that all repeat one news story are not independent confirmation, and none of them is the original.
whyWrong.D: Vaguer wording dodges the check instead of doing it. 'Most employees' could be just as wrong, and the post loses the specific evidence it needed.

questions.mindset: Trace a statistic back to whoever actually measured it, not to whoever repeated it.

questions.stem: An internal communications lead asks Claude to draft a feature on the company's history for the staff newsletter. The draft includes a vivid quote attributed to the founder: "We will never sell a product we would not use ourselves." The lead does not remember the founder ever saying this, and Claude was given no interviews or speeches to work from. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Ask Claude whether the quote is genuine, and keep it in the feature if Claude says it came from a real interview.
Keep the quote but present it as a paraphrase, since it fits the founder's well-known values and tone.
Search the web for the phrase and keep it if a quotation website attributes the same words to the founder.
Remove the quote unless it appears in a recording, transcript or publication, or the founder confirms it.

questions.explanation: Claude was given no source material, so the quote can only have come from general knowledge or invention. Hallucination-reduction techniques lower the risk of plausible-looking fabrications but do not eliminate them, and content going out under the company's name still needs validation. A quote is verified only when it appears in an **original record** — a recording, transcript or publication — or the person who supposedly said it confirms it. Otherwise it comes out.

whyWrong.A: Asking Claude to vouch for its own output is not independent evidence. It can confidently 'confirm' a quote it made up.
whyWrong.B: Calling it a paraphrase still puts words in a real person's mouth. A plausible-sounding line is exactly what a fabricated quote looks like.
whyWrong.C: Quotation websites often carry misattributed lines and are not original records. Finding the phrase there does not show the founder said it.

questions.mindset: A quote is a fact about what a real person said; verify it at the original record or cut it.

questions.stem: A logistics coordinator uploads a CSV of 4,000 shipments to Claude and asks for the average delivery time per region. Claude answers with a neat table of regional averages written into its response. The figures will be used in next month's carrier contract negotiation. Which TWO steps would MOST reliably validate the numbers? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have Claude calculate the averages by running code on the uploaded file and show the method and row counts used.
Ask Claude to reread its table and confirm that each regional average looks reasonable for that region.
Paste the same CSV into a new chat and accept the figures if the second table matches the first one closely.
Recalculate one or two regions independently in a spreadsheet and check they match the reported averages.
Ask Claude to round every average to whole days so small calculation differences do not matter in the meeting.

questions.explanation: Figures typed into a response can be estimated rather than computed. Claude can run code on an uploaded data file (Code Execution), so asking it to **actually calculate** the averages and show its method — including how many rows each region used — makes the work reproducible and checkable. An **independent spot-check** of one or two regions in a spreadsheet then confirms the method gives the right answer. Together they turn 'looks precise' into 'shown to be correct'.

whyWrong.B: A self-review checks plausibility, not arithmetic. An average can look reasonable and still be wrong.
whyWrong.C: Two runs agreeing raises confidence a little, but both can share the same mistake (for example, both silently dropping rows). Agreement is not a calculation check.
whyWrong.E: Rounding hides errors rather than finding them. A wrong average rounded to whole days is still wrong.

questions.mindset: For numbers, make the calculation real and then check it yourself, rather than trusting fluent text.

questions.stem: An IT support lead uses Claude to answer staff questions about connecting to the company VPN. Several answers describe settings menus that do not exist in the company's VPN client, because Claude is answering from general knowledge. The company has an up-to-date internal setup guide. Which change would MOST effectively make future answers accurate and easy to check?

options.text: Add the internal guide to a Project and tell Claude to answer only from it, saying 'not covered' when the guide is silent.
Tell Claude in each chat to be extra careful and accurate when describing the settings in VPN client menus.
Have Claude write longer answers that cover several common VPN clients, so the right steps are in there somewhere.
Add a note under each answer telling staff that the steps were written by AI and might not be fully correct.

questions.explanation: The facts already exist in the company's own guide, so the strongest fix is **grounding**: add the guide to a Project's knowledge so it is available in every chat, and restrict Claude to that material, with permission to say the guide doesn't cover something. Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends exactly this pair — restrict Claude to the provided documents and let it admit when it doesn't know. Each answer can then be checked against one known document.

whyWrong.B: Asking for care does not give Claude the information it is missing. It still has nothing to answer from except general knowledge.
whyWrong.C: Covering several products makes answers longer and more confusing, and staff still have to guess which steps apply to them.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer passes the checking work to every reader without fixing the cause of the wrong answers.

questions.mindset: When the facts live in your own documents, ground Claude in them instead of checking its memory.

questions.stem: A product marketing manager gives Claude three internal product briefs and asks for a one-page customer-facing overview of a new feature. The draft reads well, but she suspects a few benefits were added that are not in the briefs. She wants the quickest dependable way to strip out unsupported claims before she does her own final read. What should she do?

options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each sentence from 1 to 10 and delete any sentence that scores below 7.
Regenerate the overview several times and keep only the benefits that appear in every one of the versions.
Ask Claude to pair each claim with a direct quote from the briefs, remove any claim it cannot support, then spot-check.
Ask Claude to rewrite the overview in a more cautious tone, so that any overstated benefits sound less definite.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations describes exactly this pattern: after drafting, have Claude find a **supporting quote** for each claim and **retract** any claim it cannot support. That makes the draft auditable, because every remaining claim points to text she can check in the briefs. Her spot-check of the quotes is still the final step.

whyWrong.A: Self-rated confidence is not evidence. Claude can be very confident about a benefit the briefs never mention.
whyWrong.B: An invented benefit can show up in every version. Repetition shows consistency, not that the briefs support the claim.
whyWrong.D: A softer tone leaves unsupported claims in place. 'May help teams save time' is still wrong if the briefs never say it.

questions.mindset: Make every claim point to its evidence, and drop the ones that can't.

questions.stem: An events coordinator asks Claude for the date a professional licensing body's annual renewal period closes, so she can remind 200 members. In one chat Claude says 31 March; when she asks again in a fresh chat, it says 30 April. Both answers sound equally confident. What should she conclude, and what should she do next?

options.text: The date is uncertain, so she should use the earlier date in the reminder to be safe and not check further.
Ask a third time and use whichever date appears in two of the three answers, since that is the majority result.
Ask Claude to explain which of its two answers is correct and use the date it settles on after the explanation.
Answers that change mean neither is reliable, so she should confirm the date on the licensing body's official site.

questions.explanation: Running the same question more than once and comparing the answers is a recognized consistency check (the docs list best-of-N consistency comparison among hallucination-reduction techniques). But inconsistency only tells you there is a problem; it does not tell you which answer is right. The fix is to go to the **authoritative source** — here, the licensing body's own published dates.

whyWrong.A: Picking the earlier date is still a guess. If both dates are wrong, members get incorrect information either way.
whyWrong.B: A majority vote among unreliable answers is not verification. Two matching guesses can still both be wrong.
whyWrong.C: Claude's explanation of which answer is right is a third unverified answer, not evidence.

questions.mindset: Inconsistent answers flag a problem; only the authoritative source resolves it.

questions.stem: A policy analyst at a trade association uses Claude with web search to check a claim that a competitor "cut 1,200 jobs last quarter" before it goes into a members' briefing. Claude cites two industry news sites that both report the figure. On opening them, she notices both articles use near-identical wording and each credits "a company announcement". What is the BEST way to treat this evidence?

options.text: Treat the claim as confirmed, since two separate publications reporting the same number is independent agreement.
Treat the two sites as one source and check the company's own announcement or filing before using the figure.
Ask Claude to find a third news site that reports the figure, so the claim is backed by more than two sources.
Leave the figure out of the briefing, since news reports about job cuts are too unreliable to be used at all.

questions.explanation: Cross-checking only works when the sources are **independent**. Two articles with near-identical wording that both credit 'a company announcement' are one source reported twice; their agreement adds nothing. The company's own announcement or filing is the authoritative record, and it also carries the context — for example, whether the 1,200 includes planned roles or covers a single site. For a figure going into a members' briefing, validate it against that original record.

whyWrong.A: Near-identical wording and the same credited origin show the articles are not independent. Their agreement adds nothing beyond the original.
whyWrong.C: A third site is likely to copy the same announcement. More copies of one source are still one source.
whyWrong.D: This overreacts. The figure may be accurate and useful; it just needs checking at the original.

questions.mindset: Count sources by where the information came from, not by how many pages repeat it.

questions.stem: A grants officer at a charity uses Claude's Research feature to support a funding application. The report states "youth unemployment in the region doubled between 2019 and 2023" and links to a government statistics page. The link works. Reading the page, she finds it shows the figure doubled for the whole country, while the region rose by about a third. The application is due in two days. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.text: Correct the claim to the regional figure the source supports, or replace the citation with a source for the stated claim.
Keep the sentence because the citation links to a real government page, which reviewers will regard as credible.
Ask Claude to rewrite the sentence so it sounds less specific, such as "unemployment rose sharply", and keep the link.
Run the same Research query again and use the new report if it gives a figure that is closer to the national one.

questions.explanation: Checking a citation has three parts: the source exists, it is the source it claims to be, and **it says what the claim says**. Here the third check fails — the page supports a national figure, not a regional one. The claim must be corrected to match the evidence, or replaced with a source that actually supports it. She already has the correct regional figure in the source she opened, so the fix costs minutes, not another research run.

whyWrong.B: A working link to a credible site does not support a claim it doesn't make. A reviewer who opens the page would find the mismatch and doubt the whole application.
whyWrong.C: 'Rose sharply' still leans on a page that doesn't show it for the region, and it hides the real evidence the charity has.
whyWrong.D: Regenerating hopes for a better answer instead of using the source she already has, which tells her the correct regional figure.

questions.mindset: A real link is not support; check that the source says what the claim says, in context.

questions.stem: A small-business owner uses Claude for many tasks each week and has limited time for checking. Which TWO of these outputs MOST need every specific claim verified against an authoritative source before use? Choose TWO.

options.text: A list of twenty possible names for the team's new internal project channel, to be voted on informally at lunch.
A customer FAQ page stating refund terms, warranty length and delivery times, to be published on the website.
A rough outline of talking points for a brainstorming session that she will facilitate with her own staff.
A first draft of ideas for decorating the office for the end-of-year party, to be shared with two colleagues.
A summary of the loan terms and repayment figures from the bank's offer, which she will use to accept the loan.

questions.explanation: Fact-checking effort should be **proportionate to the stakes**. The customer FAQ is public and commits the business to terms; the loan summary feeds a binding financial decision. An error in either could cost money or trust, so every specific claim gets checked against the real policy or the bank's own offer. The docs are explicit that even with good techniques, high-stakes output must still be validated; the other three tasks are internal, informal and cheap to correct.

whyWrong.A: Internal, informal and easy to change. A weak name idea costs nothing, so line-by-line checking would waste her limited time.
whyWrong.C: A rough outline for her own facilitation is low-stakes and she will adapt it live. Heavy verification is not proportionate.
whyWrong.D: Party decoration ideas are low-stakes and reversible. There are no facts here that could cause harm if wrong.

questions.mindset: Spend verification effort where an error would be public, binding or costly.

questions.stem: Each week a team assistant uses a Claude Project to draft a client update covering open orders, delivery dates and account contacts. Over two months, three updates went out with a wrong delivery date or an outdated contact name, each caught by a different client. The team wants a fix that makes checking reliable every week with the least ongoing effort. What should they do?

options.text: Ask the most experienced team member to reread every update in full each week before it is sent to clients.
Add an instruction to the Project telling Claude to double-check all dates and names before finishing each draft.
Write a short checklist naming each fact type, the system to check it in and who signs off, and keep it in the Project.
Stop including delivery dates and contact names in the updates, so that clients can no longer receive wrong ones.

questions.explanation: For recurring work, a **repeatable validation checklist** beats heroic one-off effort. Naming which facts must be checked (delivery dates, contact names), **where** each is checked (the order system, the CRM) and **who signs off** turns a vague 'be careful' into a quick, consistent routine. Keeping the checklist in the Project's knowledge puts it next to the work every week and makes the check survive staff changes — a process fix, not a prompt tweak or a content sacrifice.

whyWrong.A: A full reread depends on one person and does not say what to check against. Reviewers miss the same errors when they don't compare with the system of record.
whyWrong.B: Claude can't check dates it doesn't have access to. A self-check instruction is not verification against the order system or CRM.
whyWrong.D: Removing the most useful content to avoid errors makes the update much less valuable to clients. The problem is checking, not the content.

questions.mindset: Turn recurring checks into a named checklist: what to verify, where, and who signs off.

questions.stem: A finance assistant asks Claude, without web search turned on, what the central bank's current base interest rate is, for a note to the leadership team today. Claude gives a precise figure. What is the BEST way to handle this answer?

options.text: Use the figure, since a precise number like this suggests Claude has reliable and recent information on the topic.
Ask Claude to confirm that the figure is still current, and use it if Claude says nothing has changed since.
Round the figure to the nearest whole percent, so the note stays roughly right even if the rate has changed slightly.
Treat it as possibly out of date and confirm it on the central bank's official site, or with web search and citations.

questions.explanation: With web search off and no document provided, the figure can only come from Claude's training knowledge, which reflects a point in time and can be out of date for anything that changes. A current base rate must be confirmed at the **authoritative source** — the central bank's own announcement — or via web search with citations she can open and check. Precision in the answer is not evidence that it is current.

whyWrong.A: Precision is not evidence of being current. An outdated figure can be stated just as precisely.
whyWrong.B: Without access to current information, Claude cannot know whether the rate has changed. Its reassurance does not check anything.
whyWrong.C: Rounding makes the number less accurate without making it current. Leaders could act on a stale figure.

questions.mindset: Anything that changes over time gets checked against a current, official source.

questions.stem: A curriculum coordinator asks Claude for a recommended reading list of eight books on project management for a staff training course. When she starts ordering, the bookshop cannot find one title, and another is listed under a different author. The list will be printed in the course handbook. Which TWO actions should she take? Choose TWO.

options.text: Check every title and author on the list in a library catalog or the publisher's site, not just the two that failed.
Ask Claude to confirm that each book on the list is real and keep the books that Claude says it is certain about.
Remove or replace any book that cannot be found in a catalog, and correct any author details to match the record.
Keep the list as it is and add a note to the handbook saying that some titles may be hard to find in shops.
Ask Claude to regenerate a new list of eight books and use that one, since the first attempt had a few errors.

questions.explanation: Two bad entries out of eight suggest the list may contain **fabricated or garbled references**, so every entry needs checking, not just the two that happened to fail. A library catalog or publisher listing is the authoritative record of title and author. Whatever cannot be found is removed or replaced with a verified book, and author details are corrected to match the record before the handbook is printed.

whyWrong.B: Claude's certainty about its own references is not verification. It can be confident about a book that doesn't exist.
whyWrong.D: A note doesn't fix a book that may not exist. Printing it would mislead every learner who tries to find it.
whyWrong.E: A fresh list has the same risk and would itself need full checking. It replaces known problems with unknown ones.

questions.mindset: When some references fail, check them all against the record and cut what can't be found.

questions.stem: A strategy associate asks Claude to assess whether the company should expand into a new region. Claude's analysis concludes the market is "large and fast-growing" and recommends expansion. Her director will use it to decide whether to fund a full feasibility study, and asks her to stress-test it first. Which approach would MOST effectively expose weak points in the conclusion?

options.text: Ask Claude to restate the recommendation more persuasively, so that the director can see how strong the case is.
Ask Claude what evidence would contradict the conclusion and what its key assumptions rest on, then verify those.
Run the analysis again with the most capable model available and adopt its conclusion if it also recommends expansion.
Ask Claude to add more supporting examples of other companies that expanded successfully into similar regions.

questions.explanation: Stress-testing means looking for what would make the conclusion **wrong**. Asking for counter-evidence and the load-bearing assumptions (market size figures, growth rate, their sources) surfaces the claims the whole recommendation depends on, and exposes one-sided, confirmation-seeking analysis. She then checks those specific claims against authoritative data. This is targeted validation, not a vote of confidence.

whyWrong.A: Making the case more persuasive hides weaknesses instead of exposing them. It's the opposite of a stress test.
whyWrong.C: A second model agreeing is not evidence. Both may rely on the same unchecked assumptions about the market.
whyWrong.D: More success stories add one-sided support and ignore companies that failed. That increases bias rather than testing the conclusion.

questions.mindset: To validate a conclusion, hunt for what would disprove it and check the assumptions it rests on.

questions.stem: A customer success manager asks Claude to summarize a quarterly retention report for the executive team. Claude writes: "Customer churn rose 3% this quarter." The report's data table shows churn went from 12% last quarter to 15% this quarter. Executives often compare quarters closely. What is the MOST appropriate fix before sending?

options.text: Leave the sentence as written, because 15 minus 12 is 3, so the summary already matches the report's numbers.
Change it to "churn rose 25%" because that relative change is the more dramatic and more useful figure for executives.
Recheck the source table and state both rates: "churn rose from 12% to 15%, an increase of 3 percentage points".
Ask Claude to review the sentence for accuracy and accept its version if it confirms that the 3% figure is right.

questions.explanation: "Rose 3%" is ambiguous: it can be read as 3 **percentage points** (12% to 15%, which is what happened) or as a 3% **relative** rise (12% to about 12.4%, which would understate the change badly). Recalculating from the source table and stating the starting and ending values with the correct unit makes the claim both accurate and checkable. Percentages attached to the wrong base are a common way that fluent summaries mislead.

whyWrong.A: The arithmetic is right but the wording is ambiguous. A reader can take '3%' as a small relative rise and badly underestimate the problem.
whyWrong.B: 25% is correct as a relative change, but on its own it hides the actual rates, and choosing the more dramatic number is a framing choice, not a validation.
whyWrong.D: Claude may well 'confirm' its own wording. The problem is ambiguity in the claim, which only checking it against the source and restating it fixes.

questions.mindset: Recompute from the source and state numbers so they can't be misread: values plus the right unit.

questions.stem: A procurement coordinator uploads a 90-page supplier agreement and asks Claude what notice the company must give to end the contract early. Claude answers "60 days' written notice". She needs to rely on this when advising her manager, and wants the answer to be checkable without reading all 90 pages. Which TWO actions would BEST achieve this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude how confident it is in the 60-day answer and accept it if Claude reports high confidence in the figure.
Ask Claude to quote word for word the clauses on early termination and notice, with their section numbers.
Ask Claude to shorten its answer to a single line so her manager receives a clear and simple figure to act on.
Open the agreement at those section numbers and confirm the quoted wording and any exceptions or conditions.
Ask the same question in a fresh chat with the agreement and accept the figure if both answers say 60 days.

questions.explanation: For long documents, Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends having Claude extract **word-for-word quotes** first and answer from them. Asking for the clauses on early termination and notice, with section numbers, grounds the answer in the actual text and gives her exact places to look. Opening the agreement at those sections to confirm the wording — and any conditions, such as a different notice period in the first year — means checking a few paragraphs instead of 90 pages, and the answer is backed by the document itself.

whyWrong.A: Confidence is not evidence. A confident answer can still miss an exception elsewhere in the agreement.
whyWrong.C: A shorter answer is easier to read but no easier to check. It may also drop conditions that matter.
whyWrong.E: Matching answers from two runs can repeat the same misreading. Agreement is a weak signal, not a check against the clause.

questions.mindset: Ask for exact quotes with locations, then check them: verification in minutes, not hours.
